title: The association between the acute:chronic workload ratio and injury and its application in team sports: a systematic review
authors: Griffin A, Kenny IC, Comyns TM, Lyons M
population: 22 studies of team-sport athletes examining ACWR and injury
findings: 22 articles met inclusion criteria; median Newcastle-Ottawa Scale score 8 (range 5-9).
Review supports an association between ACWR and non-contact injuries and its use as one tool in a larger multifaceted monitoring system.
Support exists for both rolling-average and EWMA models; EWMA is judged more suitable, in part for greater sensitivity.
The most appropriate acute and chronic windows and load variables may depend on the sport.
22 articles met inclusion; median Newcastle-Ottawa quality score 8 (range 5-9).
The review reports it supports an association between ACWR and non-contact injuries, and its use as one tool within a larger multifaceted monitoring system that includes other proven methods.
Both rolling-average and exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) models were supported; EWMA is described as more suitable, partly for greater sensitivity.
The most appropriate acute and chronic windows and load variables may depend on the sport; future work should cover both sexes and combine ACWR with other risk factors.
limitations: Team sports only, no endurance running. Observational cohorts with heterogeneous ACWR definitions. Association, not causation; predates the main critiques (Impellizzeri 2020, Wang 2020).
implications: Evidence for ACWR comes from team sports; do not transfer a 0.8-1.3 'sweet spot' to running plans.
If ACWR is ever surfaced, use EWMA, label it a monitoring signal, and combine with other risk factors.
No change to plan generation is justified by this paper alone.
ACWR evidence is contested: associations exist in team sports but causal use is unsupported, so at most show it as a descriptive monitor.
If a ratio is displayed, an EWMA formulation is the better-supported option over rolling averages, and it must sit inside a multi-signal view rather than act alone.

verification.notes: Crossref: Sports Med 50:561-580 (online Nov 2019), 4 authors. Abstract matched. Grade A reflects design; applicability to running is low.
